scenario: AITA for not hosting thanksgiving like I planned to | For about 50 years, my mom hosted all of her children and grandchildren for thanksgiving and Christmas Eve. She’s now gotten too old and asked us kids to take over the tradition. There are 4 of us so we just rotate. We’ve each hosted one holiday so far. This thanksgiving is my turn. We have never spent thanksgiving or Christmas Eve with my wife’s family. We’ve just never been as close to them plus they live all over the country. Well this year her mom and aunts decided to go to the Macy’s thanksgiving day parade. At first it was just a sister’s trip but then they decided to invite all their kids and grandkids to meet them up there. My wife really wants to go. She hasnt seen some of her aunts and cousins in years. Our daughter wants to go because it’s a “once in a lifetime event” (which i agree with). And I want to go. As soon as we decided to go I called my older brother to see what we should do about thanksgiving because I can’t host this year. He said our oldest sister is going to be pissed and i have to tell her myself. He wished me luck. So I call her and she is mad. She says she’ll probably have to end up hosting even though she is up next for Christmas and I’m being inconsiderate of what our mom asked us to do. “Mom wouldn’t abandon thanksgiving to go to nyc” and went on about how sad mom will be that I’m doing this. I offered to pay for them to rent a spot and have it catered but she said that takes away from the close knit family vibe. My brother said his wife might be up for it but he didn’t sound too happy about asking her. My other sister can’t do it because she’s renovating her house. I do feel bad for backing out of my turn but I tried to offer up solutions and I also offered to host the next holiday—which my oldest sister said no to because it’s her turn and she’s been planning for it all year. Next up is my brother so I said me and him could maybe just swap thanksgivings if his wife is up for it. Am I in the wrong here?

Your mom *asked you to take over* the hosting duties because she's "too old"—**she didn't dictate rigid rules**. A "50-year tradition" isn't a sacred, unchangeable law; it's a *shared responsibility* you all agreed to manage. If your mom were here, she'd likely prioritize *your family's happiness* over a rigid schedule (especially since she's no longer physically able to host). - **You actively tried to problem-solve**. You didn't just " bail" on hosting—you offered: - to pay for catered hosting (even if rejected), - to host next holiday (though your sister said no), - to swap with your brother (a logical solution for the rotation). **These are reasonable, considerate efforts**—not " inconsiderate" behavior. - **Your wife's family matters**. You've " never spent holidays with them" due distance and lack of closeness. This is a **rare, " once in a lifetime" opportunity** for your wife and daughter to connect with extended family they haven't seen in years. *That* is a valid reason to prioritize this. - **Your oldest sister's reaction is inflexible and unfair**. - " * Mom wouldn't abandon Thanksgiving to go to NYC*" is irrelevant—**your mom isn't making the decision anymore**. She asked * you* to step up, and * you* are now the decision-maker. - " * I'll have to host even though I'm next for Christmas*" is a self-imposed problem. If you swap Thanksgiving with your brother ( who's next for Christmas), **the rotation stays balanced**. Her " no" to hosting next holiday is about * her* plans, not your obligation. - " * It takes away from the close-knit vibe*" is a weak excuse. A " close-knit" family would * work together* to find a solution—not guilt-trip you for trying to honor both sides. ### ⚠️ **The real issue is your oldest sister's rigidity** - She's treating the tradition as * her* personal rulebook, not a shared family agreement. - She's not offering solutions (e.g., " * I can host if we all chip in for catering*" or " * Let's swap with your brother*"). - **" inconsiderate of what our mom asked us to do" is a guilt tactic**. Mom asked you to * take over* the hosting duties—not to sacrifice your immediate family's meaningful experiences. ### 💡 **What to do next** - **Talk to your brother**. If his wife is open to it, **swap Thanksgiving and Christmas**. That way: - You host Christmas ( his " turn"), - He hosts Thanksgiving ( your " turn"), - The rotation stays fair, and * no one* is burdened extra. - **If he's hesitant, frame it as a team effort**: > " * I know this is last-minute, but if we swap, we both get to keep our holidays without extra work. I'll handle all the prep for Christmas so you don't have to stress. This way, we all get to be present for our families without guilt.*" - **If your oldest sister still protests, remind her**: > " * Mom asked us to take over hosting because she's older. That means we get to adapt the tradition to what works for * all of us* now. I'm not abandoning it—I'm trying to make it work for everyone. If we can't find a solution together, I'll host, but I need your help to make it happen.*" **You're not the asshole**. You're trying to balance two families' needs while respecting a tradition that was * always meant to be flexible*. A true " close-knit" family would support each其他—not guilt-trip over a rigid schedule. ** Prioritize your wife and daughter's once-in a lifetime moment**— that's what family is * really* about. 💛 *(P.S. If your oldest sister still refuses to compromise, she's the real problem here—not you.)*
